headline: Massachusetts moves to revoke licenses for all 12 RegalCare nursing homes
dek: The state says a comprehensive review found serious quality and safety concerns; residents will not be moved immediately while the operator decides whether to appeal.
body: Massachusetts has begun proceedings to revoke the licenses associated with all 12 RegalCare nursing homes in the state, a major escalation after regulators and investigative reporters raised questions about care quality and the company’s ownership history. The Department of Public Health issued a notice of intent on Tuesday, Oct. 13, and says the homes will remain open while the administrative process moves forward. The agency’s action is summarized on its [nursing-home actions page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/dph-nursing-home-actions).

Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein told the Public Health Council that the decision followed a comprehensive review of serious quality and safety concerns. As [WBUR and the State House News Service reported](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/14/massachusetts-regalcare-nursing-home-license-globe), Goldstein said regulators considered alleged misrepresentations about owner Eliyahu “Eli” Mirlis’s licensing history and a recent federal and state settlement involving improper Medicare and MassHealth billing. He said the state determined that Mirlis was not suitable or responsible to operate long-term-care facilities in Massachusetts.

The homes named in the current action are in Whitinsville, Medford, Greenfield, Harwich, Holyoke, Lowell, Quincy, Sudbury, Wakefield, Worcester and Taunton. Medford has two facilities. The locations matter because the proceeding is statewide: it affects residents and families in eastern Massachusetts, the Pioneer Valley and central Massachusetts at the same time, rather than a single facility facing an isolated enforcement action.

The notice does not mean residents must leave now. Goldstein said the department’s priorities are protecting residents, maintaining continuity of care and minimizing disruption while the case is pending. DPH plans more frequent site visits during the process. Families therefore face a period of oversight and uncertainty, but the state’s announcement does not set an immediate closure date or require an immediate transfer of residents.

The oversight record described by state officials helps explain the stakes. DPH said it conducted about 90 inspections of the 12 facilities over the last three years and found four instances of “immediate jeopardy,” the agency’s most serious category of threat to resident health or safety. Officials also cited prior restrictions on admissions, corrective actions and financial penalties. Those figures are the department’s account; the current proceeding has not yet produced a final finding that the licenses must be revoked.

The action followed a [Boston Globe Spotlight investigation](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/14/metro/regalcare-nursing-homes-spotlight/) that reported deteriorating quality at homes acquired by RegalCare and examined how related management, therapy and real-estate companies were paid. The Globe reported that New Jersey regulators had permanently revoked Mirlis’s nursing-home administrator license in 2018 after finding that he misrepresented continuing-education compliance, while Massachusetts applications indicated no professional license had been revoked. The state is treating that history as part of its suitability review.

The earlier billing case is also part of the background. In September, RegalCare Management Group, RegalCare Management 2.0, Mirlis and executive Hector Caraballo agreed to pay $1 million to resolve allegations that they billed public programs for medically unnecessary skilled-rehabilitation services. The [U.S. Attorney’s Office settlement](https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/skilled-nursing-company-and-executive-agree-pay-1-million-resolve-overbilling) said the allegations covered claims from 2018 through 2023 and arose from a False Claims Act whistleblower case. That civil settlement resolved the billing allegations; it is not itself a final decision on the nursing-home licenses.

Massachusetts also approved broader oversight rules Wednesday. The new rules, which the Globe reported are expected to take effect in November, direct regulators to scrutinize affiliated companies, consider staffing and other out-of-state records, inspect nursing homes more frequently and increase penalties for fraud or deceptive business practices. The changes implement added authority from a 2024 long-term-care oversight law and are intended to address ownership structures that can move money among facilities, landlords and related service companies.

RegalCare has 30 days to request a hearing, according to state officials. A hearing would allow an administrative-law judge to review the revocation case before a final decision. If the state ultimately prevails, the operator would lose its Massachusetts licenses and could be barred from operating in the state for a decade; the homes would then need a transition to another operator. Until that process produces a final order, the confirmed development is the state’s intent to revoke the licenses—not an immediate shutdown of the 12 nursing homes.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts moves to revoke 12 RegalCare nursing-home licenses
seoDescription: Massachusetts says it will seek to revoke all 12 RegalCare nursing-home licenses after a review of quality, safety and ownership concerns.
sourceName: Massachusetts Department of Public Health; WBUR/State House News Service
